history: Jacob Grohusko printed it in 1908. It calls for Amer Picon, which has not been legally imported to the US in decades—every modern Brooklyn is an approximation.
whyItWorks: Dry vermouth keeps it lean where a Manhattan is round; the amaro supplies the bitter orange spine that holds the rye up.
steps: Stir everything with ice until well chilled.
techniqueNotes: Amer Picon is the historical call. Averna, Ramazzotti or a bar-made Picon substitute all work; say which you used.

recommendedBottles.rationale: Peppery enough to stand up to the amaro.
Rounder, if you want the maraschino forward.

substitutions.notes: Any bitter orange amaro. Cynar takes it savory.
Bourbon makes it sweeter and blunter—closer to a Manhattan.

name: Brooklyn
description: Manhattan's overlooked sibling: rye and dry vermouth, with maraschino and bitter amaro doing the sweetening.
